results.result: V1 ChCs receive monosynaptic input predominantly from local L5 pyramidal cells and from higher-order cortical regions including RSC, with L5 inputs being excitatory. This connectivity pattern differs from prefrontal cortex ChCs but resembles S1 ChCs.
results.evaluation: The rabies tracing experiments (C1, C15, Figure 1C) clearly demonstrate L5 as the primary local input source. Optogenetic validation with TTX/4-AP confirms monosynaptic RSC inputs (C19-C21, Figure 1H). Morphological analysis confirms excitatory nature of L5 inputs (C16). The comparison with other brain regions is appropriately cited (C17-C18). Sample sizes are modest (n=4 mice, 30 starter cells) but adequate for tracing studies.

results.result: ChCs exhibit non-reciprocal connectivity with L2/3 PyCs: ChCs innervate ~45% of nearby PyCs, but receive no detectable input from L2/3 PyCs. Local L1-4 inputs to ChCs likely originate from inhibitory interneurons.
results.evaluation: Paired recordings (n=11 pairs) demonstrate clear asymmetry: 5/11 ChC→PyC connections but 0/11 PyC→ChC connections (C24-C25, Figure 1K). The inference about inhibitory inputs (C28) is reasonable given the lack of PyC inputs and consistency with prior literature (C29). However, the sample size is relatively small and the use of high chloride internal solution prevents determining whether ChC inputs are hyperpolarizing or depolarizing.

results.result: ChCs are visually responsive but show weak orientation selectivity compared to PyCs. They are highly active during arousal states and show synchronized activity with high within-cell-type correlations.
results.evaluation: Calcium imaging data demonstrate visual responses (Figure 2D-E) with significantly lower OSI than PyCs (C34, Figure 2G, LMEM statistics provided). High correlations with running speed and pupil size (C31, Figure 2B-C) and between ChCs (C32) are well-documented. Sample sizes are adequate (n=1883 PyCs, 95 ChCs from 8 mice). Statistical analyses using LMEM appropriately account for hierarchical data structure.

results.result: ChCs show weak selectivity for natural images with low sparsity, high between-cell correlations, and poor decoding accuracy. CNN modeling reveals they have lower OSI, contrast sensitivity, prefer lower spatial frequencies, and have larger receptive fields than PyCs. These properties are consistent with convergent input from many L5 PyCs with diverse tuning.
results.evaluation: Natural image responses (n=34 ChCs, 1015 L2/3 PyCs, 1601 L5 PyCs) show significantly lower sparsity (C38, Figure 3C) and decoding accuracy (C40, Figure 3E, permutation test p<0.001). CNN modeling provides converging evidence for weak selectivity (C41-C44, Figure 3G-J). The mechanistic interpretation linking properties to L5 PyC convergence (C45, C87, C90) is reasonable but speculative. The composite L5 PyC MEI analysis (Figure 3—supplement 1F) provides supporting evidence but doesn't exclude alternatives.

results.result: In a virtual tunnel paradigm, ChCs respond strongly to locomotion and visuomotor mismatch but are suppressed by visual stimuli. They correlate more strongly with non-visual PyCs (NV-PyCs) than visual PyCs (V-PyCs), supporting the existence of functionally distinct PyC populations.
results.evaluation: Virtual tunnel experiments (n=1256 PyCs, 38 ChCs from 6 mice) demonstrate strong ChC responses to locomotion onset (C4, Figure 4F,J) and visuomotor mismatch (C5, Figure 4E,I) with visual suppression (C46, Figure 4C-D). Hierarchical clustering identifies two PyC populations (C48, Figure 4C-D), validated by permutation testing showing separability exceeds chance (C49, Figure 4—supplement 1F, p<0.001). Higher ChC-NV-PyC correlations are statistically significant (C53, Figure 4K). PV+ ChC validation (C54) strengthens conclusions. Open vs. closed loop comparisons (C55-C56) appropriately control for sensory vs. sensorimotor effects.

results.result: Repeated exposure to the virtual tunnel induces experience-dependent plasticity in ChCs, with significantly reduced visual responses after training. NV-PyCs also show reduced responses, while V-PyCs are unchanged. ChC pairwise correlations decrease after training.
results.evaluation: Chronic imaging of matched neurons (n=411 PyCs, 51 ChCs from 5 mice) shows significant reduction in ChC visual responses after training (C6, C58, Figure 5B-D, LMEM p<0.05) while PyC responses are unchanged (C59, Figure 5D). Orientation and direction selectivity remain stable (C60). Separate analysis of matched V-PyCs and NV-PyCs (n=68 V-PyCs, 71 NV-PyCs from 3 mice) confirms NV-PyC plasticity (C61, Figure 5E-G). Reduced ChC correlations after training (C62, p<0.01) align with PFC findings. The interpretation that plasticity generalizes across visual stimuli (C63) is reasonable given different stimuli in training vs. testing.

results.result: Visuomotor training induces structural plasticity at ChC-AIS synapses: increased fraction of AISs contacted by ChCs, decreased AIS length, increased ChC bouton density, and boutons positioned closer to AIS base. The number of boutons per contacted AIS remains constant.
results.evaluation: Immunohistochemistry (n=5 naive, 3-5 trained mice, 1802-1802 AISs analyzed) demonstrates increased fraction of contacted AISs (C65, Figure 6D, χ²-test p<0.001), decreased AIS length (C66, Figure 6E-F, LMEM p<0.05), increased bouton density (C67, Figure 6G, p<0.05), and proximal bouton shift (C68, Figure 6H-I, p<0.05), while boutons per AIS remain constant (C64, Figure 6B-C). These findings align with prior work in premotor cortex and S1 (C115). The structural changes are well-quantified with appropriate statistics, though the functional consequences remain speculative.

results.result: Chemogenetic silencing of ChCs produces only weak effects on PyC activity: mild overall activity increase, increased intercept but unchanged slope of locomotion modulation, and only 21% of PyCs showing significant activity increases. ChCs do not differentially target PyCs based on locomotion modulation.
results.evaluation: KORD-mediated ChC silencing (n=84 ChCs, 1669 PyCs from 12 mice) shows strong ChC suppression but only mild PyC activation (C70, Figure 7B, LMEM p<0.01 for PyCs). Linear modeling reveals increased intercept but unchanged slope (C71, Figure 7D-E), suggesting tonic rather than gain modulation. Only 21% vs. 13% control show increased activity (C72, χ²-test p<0.001). No correlation between locomotion modulation and silencing effect (C73, r=0.0068, p=0.78). Control experiments (n=37 ChCs, 968 PyCs from 7 mice) show no effects. These findings challenge the notion of powerful ChC control but are consistent with computational predictions (C118).

results.result: ChCs may provide an arousal-related signal that modulates PyC activity and/or gates AIS plasticity during behaviorally relevant events, though they appear unsuited for computing high-dimensional prediction errors.
results.evaluation: This interpretive result synthesizes multiple observations: arousal-related activity (C10, supported by Figures 2-4), weak inhibitory effects (C11, Figure 7), and structural plasticity (C12, Figure 6). However, the mechanistic proposals are largely speculative (C108, C112, C113, C125). The argument against prediction error coding (C109-C110) is logical given weak inhibition and high correlations, but the alternative gating hypothesis lacks direct experimental support. The claims appropriately use tentative language ('may', 'could') but require additional experiments to test causality.

results.result: The mechanisms underlying ChC response plasticity remain unclear but could involve changes in excitatory/inhibitory balance, L5 PyC response properties, or arousal-related neuromodulation. Noradrenergic inputs may be involved but were not detected in rabies tracing.
results.evaluation: Multiple mechanistic hypotheses are proposed (C93-C96, C98) but all are explicitly speculative without direct experimental tests. The arousal hypothesis (C96, C98) is plausible given prior literature (C97, C99-C100) and the observation that trained mice habituate to visual stimuli. The absence of neuromodulatory inputs in rabies tracing (C101) is noted, with a reasonable explanation offered (C102), but this negative result is difficult to interpret definitively. These remain open questions requiring future investigation.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that most L2/3 PyCs receive variable ChC input, L2/3 PyCs respond to visuomotor mismatch, AIS shortening reduces excitability, and ChC boutons align with cisternal organelles implicated in AIS plasticity.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize relevant prior work (C81-C82: Schneider-Mizell et al., 2021; C104-C107: predictive coding literature; C111: Jordan and Keller, 2023; C121-C122: Jamann et al., 2021; C123-C124: EM studies). The citations are appropriate and the knowledge claims are accurately represented. This contextual information appropriately frames the current findings.

results.result: Repeated optogenetic stimulation of RSC inputs to ChCs at 20 Hz produces synaptic depression, suggesting high release probability.
results.evaluation: The observation of synaptic depression is clearly demonstrated (C22, Figure 1I, n=8 cells). The inference about high release probability (C23) follows established principles (Zucker and Regehr, 2002) where short-term depression typically indicates high initial release probability. However, other factors (e.g., postsynaptic receptor desensitization, presynaptic calcium dynamics) could also contribute to depression, so the interpretation, while reasonable, is not definitive.

results.result: V1 ChC connectivity is non-reciprocal like prelimbic cortex, but differs in receiving input from L5 rather than deep L3 PyCs.
results.evaluation: The comparison with prelimbic cortex (Lu et al., 2017) is appropriate and accurately represents both similarities (non-reciprocal connectivity, C84) and differences (layer of PyC input, C85). The current data (Figure 1) clearly support the V1 connectivity pattern. This comparative analysis provides valuable context for understanding regional specialization of ChC circuits.

results.result: ChCs in V1 receive monosynaptic input predominantly from local layer 5 pyramidal cells and from higher-order cortical regions (RSC, S1) and thalamic nuclei, as demonstrated by retrograde rabies tracing and optogenetic validation experiments.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states this work shows 'compelling evidence that Chandelier cells in the visual cortex receive inputs most prominently from local layer 5 pyramidal neurons.' Reviewer 1 lists as a main finding 'the identification of synaptic inputs to ChC, with a majority of local, deep layer principal neurons' and states findings are 'strongly supported by experimental data.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the primary source of input to ChCs are local layer 5 pyramidal cells, as well as long-range thalamic and cortical connections' and notes 'their analyses and statistical tests are sound.'

results.result: ChCs provide GABAergic output to local L2/3 pyramidal cells in a non-reciprocal connectivity pattern, with ChCs innervating PyCs but receiving no reciprocal connections from L2/3 PyCs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this connectivity finding without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'found that...ChCs provided input to local layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, but did not receive reciprocal connections' and states 'their analyses and statistical tests are sound.' Reviewer 1 describes this as part of the well-supported main findings with 'no major flaws.'

results.result: ChCs are visually responsive but weakly selective for stimulus content, showing lower orientation selectivity, sparsity, and decoding accuracy than pyramidal cells, while being highly correlated with arousal markers (locomotion and pupil size) and synchronized with each other.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these functional characterization findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the demonstration that ChC is strongly and synchronously activated by visual stimuli with low specificity in naive animals' is strongly supported. Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors showed that ChCs exhibit weakly selective visual responses, high correlations within their own population, and strong responses during periods of arousal' and confirms 'their results are in line with previous findings.' However, Reviewer 2 notes 'some of the results (e.g. arousal-related responses) are not entirely surprising given that similar results exist in other cortical areas,' suggesting incremental rather than novel contribution for some aspects.

results.result: ChCs respond strongly to arousal-inducing events including locomotion onset and visuomotor mismatch (when visual flow stops during running), while being suppressed by visual stimuli in trained mice, and are more correlated with a subset of pyramidal cells (NV-PyCs) that show similar response patterns.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states the work shows 'compelling evidence that...Chandelier cells...respond massively to visuomotor mismatch.' Reviewer 1 lists 'the recruitment of ChC by arousal/visuomotor mismatch' as a main finding that is 'strongly supported by experimental data.' Reviewer 2 confirms the authors 'employed a learned visuomotor task in a virtual corridor to show that ChCs exhibit strong responses to mismatches between visual flow and locomotion' and notes the methodology and analyses are sound.

results.result: Repeated exposure to the virtual tunnel induced experience-dependent plasticity in ChCs, with significantly reduced visual responses to gratings after training (while PyC responses remained unchanged), and reduced pairwise correlations among ChCs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this plasticity finding. Reviewer 1 states 'the induction of functional and structural plasticity at the ChC-PN module' is strongly supported. The editor notes the work 'indicates that visual experience in the virtual tunnel activates a plasticity mechanism in Chandelier cells' but adds 'although a specific control is lacking for this conclusion,' indicating some uncertainty about the specific mechanism. Reviewer 2 notes 'additional controls would be required to identify which component(s) of the experimental paradigm led to the functional and anatomical changes observed.'

results.result: Visuomotor training induced structural plasticity at ChC-PyC synapses, including increased fraction of AISs contacted by ChCs, increased ChC bouton density, AIS shortening in PyCs, and ChC boutons localized closer to the AIS base.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these structural plasticity findings. Reviewer 1 explicitly lists 'the induction of functional and structural plasticity at the ChC-PN module' as strongly supported. The editor acknowledges the plasticity mechanism is activated by experience, though notes controls are lacking to identify the specific causal component. Reviewer 2 similarly states 'additional controls would be required to identify which component(s) of the experimental paradigm led to the functional and anatomical changes' but does not challenge the observations themselves.

results.result: ChCs only weakly inhibit L2/3 pyramidal cells in vivo, with chemogenetic silencing producing only mild increases in PyC activity (21% of PyCs significantly increased) and affecting primarily the baseline activity rather than locomotion modulation.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states the work shows 'compelling evidence that Chandelier cells...only mildly inhibit L2/3 pyramidal neurons.' Reviewer 1 lists 'the weak disinhibition of PNs induced by ChCs silencing' as a main finding that is 'strongly supported by experimental data' and notes 'this is an impressive study and an excellent manuscript, that presents no major flaws.' Reviewer 2 confirms the methodology is comprehensive and 'their analyses and statistical tests are sound.'

results.result: ChCs may provide an arousal-related signal that modulates pyramidal cell activity and/or gates plasticity of axon initial segments during behaviorally relevant events, potentially through control of AIS geometric modifications.
results.evaluation: These are speculative interpretive claims about ChC function. While reviewers do not explicitly challenge these interpretations, they are presented as possibilities ('may modulate,' 'could regulate') rather than demonstrated mechanisms. The editor notes 'a specific control is lacking' for understanding the plasticity mechanism. Reviewer 2 states 'additional controls would be required to identify which component(s) of the experimental paradigm led to the functional and anatomical changes,' indicating the mechanistic understanding remains incomplete.

results.result: CNN modeling suggests ChC response properties (low selectivity, large receptive fields, low orientation tuning, weak contrast tuning) could result from convergent input from many L5 PyCs with diverse tuning properties, as MEIs optimized for L5 PyC combinations resemble ChC MEIs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'the authors bring a comprehensive, state-of-the-art methodology to bear, including...deep neural networks' and states 'their analyses and statistical tests are sound and for the most part, support their claims.' Reviewer 1 notes the manuscript presents findings that are 'thoroughly compared to available evidence' with no major flaws. The modeling approach and conclusions are not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: 87% of labeled neurons in Vipr2-Cre mice were identified as ChCs based on morphological properties (cell bodies at L1/L2 border and L1 dendrites).
results.evaluation: This methodological validation claim is not questioned by any reviewer. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'leveraged the development of a transgenic mouse line selective for ChC' and that experiments were 'well executed.' Reviewer 2 confirms the methodology is comprehensive and sound.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering revealed two functionally distinct clusters of L2/3 PyCs with opposite activity patterns in the virtual tunnel (V-PyCs activated by visual stimuli, NV-PyCs activated in non-visual sections), with separability higher than expected by chance.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly describes this finding: 'They also showed the existence of two clusters of pyramidal neurons with functionally different responses - a cluster with "classically visual" responses and a cluster with locomotion- and mismatch-driven responses.' The analyses are described as sound, and no reviewer challenges this clustering result.

results.result: PV+ ChCs showed identical activity patterns to Vipr2-ChCs in the virtual tunnel paradigm.
results.evaluation: This validation finding is not questioned by reviewers. It serves as a control confirming that the observed ChC activity patterns are not specific to the Vipr2-Cre labeling approach. Reviewer 1 notes experiments were 'well executed' and Reviewer 2 confirms analyses are sound.

results.result: Open-loop visual flow manipulations (independent of locomotion) produced much weaker ChC responses than closed-loop visuomotor mismatch, and onset of visual flow when stationary suppressed ChC activity.
results.evaluation: These control experiments are not challenged by reviewers and support the interpretation that ChC responses depend on visuomotor coupling rather than visual changes alone. Reviewer 2 notes the methodology is comprehensive and analyses are sound.

results.result: Orientation selectivity index (OSI) and direction selectivity index (DSI) were unchanged after virtual tunnel training for both ChCs and PyCs.
results.evaluation: This negative result is reported with statistical support and is not questioned by reviewers. It helps characterize the specificity of the training-induced plasticity effects. Reviewer 2 confirms 'their analyses and statistical tests are sound.'

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the finding that L5 pyramidal neurons are the primary local input to ChCs (C1, C14, C15, C16, C19-C21, C30). OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment of rabies tracing and optogenetics, while peer reviewers emphasize the compelling nature of the evidence. OpenEval includes additional claims (C2, C13, C17-C18, C22-C23) about RSC inputs and synaptic properties not explicitly mentioned in peer evaluation. Peer review includes C75, C85, C86 not in OpenEval's result.

Both support the asymmetric connectivity finding (C24-C27, C83): ChCs connect to PyCs but not vice versa. OpenEval notes the modest sample size (n=11 pairs) and technical limitation of high chloride internal solution, while peer reviewers accept the finding without methodological concerns. Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. Peer review includes C30, C84 not in OpenEval's result.

Both support ChC visual response properties including low orientation selectivity (C3, C31-C34, C76). However, peer review (R3) also includes natural image response claims (C36-C44) that OpenEval addresses separately in R4. Peer reviewer notes some findings are incremental rather than novel, while OpenEval focuses on statistical rigor and sample sizes. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R4 addresses natural image responses and CNN modeling (C36-C45, C86-C91), which peer review R3 partially covers (C36-C44). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of decoding accuracy and mechanistic interpretations, noting they are reasonable but speculative. Peer review confirms results align with previous findings but notes incremental contribution. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both address the mechanistic interpretation linking ChC properties to L5 PyC convergence (C45, C87-C91). OpenEval notes the CNN modeling provides converging evidence but mechanistic claims are speculative. Peer review explicitly affirms the deep neural network methodology is comprehensive and sound. Both rate as SUPPORTED for the modeling approach.

Both strongly support ChC responses to visuomotor mismatch and locomotion (C4-C5, C46, C50-C53, C57, C77). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation including hierarchical clustering and permutation testing. Peer reviewers describe evidence as compelling. OpenEval includes additional claims about PyC populations (C48-C49) and controls (C54-C56) addressed separately in peer review. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R5 includes hierarchical clustering of PyC populations (C48-C49) as part of broader visuomotor mismatch analysis. Peer review R11 addresses this clustering separately, explicitly describing two functionally different PyC clusters. Both support the finding with no challenges to the clustering methodology.

OpenEval R5 includes PV+ ChC validation (C54) as supporting evidence for visuomotor mismatch responses. Peer review R12 addresses this validation separately, confirming it as a control for the Vipr2-Cre labeling approach. Both accept the finding without question.

OpenEval R5 includes open vs. closed loop controls (C55-C56) as part of visuomotor mismatch analysis. Peer review R13 addresses these controls separately, confirming they support the interpretation that responses depend on visuomotor coupling. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both support training-induced functional plasticity in ChCs (C6, C58-C59, C61-C63, C78, C92). OpenEval provides detailed statistical assessment of chronic imaging data. Peer reviewers affirm the finding but note (via editor and Reviewer 2) that specific controls are lacking to identify which experimental component caused the plasticity. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED; peer review also SUPPORTED but with noted caveats about mechanistic specificity.

OpenEval R6 includes the finding that orientation/direction selectivity remain stable after training (C60). Peer review R14 addresses this negative result separately, confirming it helps characterize plasticity specificity. Both accept the finding as SUPPORTED.

Both support structural plasticity findings (C7, C64-C69, C79, C114). OpenEval provides detailed quantification of immunohistochemistry results with specific statistics. Peer reviewers accept the observations but note (similar to functional plasticity) that controls are lacking to identify the specific causal component. Both rate as SUPPORTED for the observations themselves, with OpenEval noting functional consequences remain speculative.

Both strongly support the finding that ChC silencing produces only mild PyC disinhibition (C9, C70-C74, C80, C117-C120, C128). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of KORD experiments and linear modeling showing tonic rather than gain modulation. Peer reviewers describe evidence as compelling with no major flaws. Both rate as SUPPORTED and note this challenges assumptions about powerful ChC control.

Both address interpretive/mechanistic claims about ChC function (C10-C12, C108-C113, C125). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting proposals are largely speculative and use tentative language but lack direct experimental support. Peer review also rates as UNCERTAIN, noting specific controls are lacking for understanding mechanisms. Both agree the mechanistic understanding remains incomplete.

OpenEval R10 addresses speculative mechanistic hypotheses about arousal and neuromodulation (C93-C103). These claims are rated UNCERTAIN as they lack direct experimental tests. No corresponding peer review result explicitly evaluates these specific mechanistic proposals, though peer reviewers generally note that mechanistic understanding requires additional controls.

OpenEval R11 addresses contextual claims accurately summarizing prior literature (C81-C82, C104-C107, C111, C121-C124). These are rated SUPPORTED as accurate representations of cited work. No corresponding peer review result explicitly evaluates these literature summary claims, though reviewers note findings are 'thoroughly compared to available evidence.'

OpenEval R12 addresses synaptic depression and inference about high release probability (C22-C23). Rated SUPPORTED with caveat that interpretation is reasonable but not definitive. No corresponding peer review result explicitly evaluates these specific claims about synaptic properties.

OpenEval R13 addresses comparison with prelimbic cortex (C84-C85), noting similarities and differences in connectivity patterns. Peer review R2 includes C84 as part of the asymmetric connectivity evaluation. Both support the comparative analysis, though peer review doesn't explicitly discuss the regional comparison.

OpenEval R13 includes C85 (layer differences between V1 and prelimbic cortex). Peer review R1 includes C85 as part of the broader input characterization. Both support the finding, with OpenEval providing explicit comparative context.

OpenEval R1 includes methodological validation of Vipr2-IRES2-Cre line (C13). Peer review R10 addresses this separately, confirming the transgenic line is selective for ChCs and experiments were well executed. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Peer review R9 explicitly affirms the CNN/deep neural network methodology (C45, C87-C91) as comprehensive and sound. This overlaps with OpenEval R4, which addresses these claims as part of natural image response analysis. Both evaluations support the modeling approach.
